name: Round pool volume
seoDesc: Round pool volume: work out depth 1 from the diameter and the width. A free construction calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: Give the Round pool volume calculator the diameter, the width, the pool volume and the water cost (for this oval pool) and it returns depth 1. Think of it as a shortcut for a materials order or a planning estimate you want to get roughly right first time. Nothing repaints underneath you: edit a field, press Calculate, and the new answer appears. That is how you find out which input the result is sensitive to.

sections.title: How does the Round pool volume calculator work?
sections.html:
The Round pool volume calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports depth 1 in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the pool type and the pool shape); then you type in the diameter (length), the width, the pool volume (Pool dimensions) and the water cost (for this oval pool) (Water cost).

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Round pool volume calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Depth 1=8 × pool volume ÷ (PI × (diameter (length) ^ 2)) − depth 2
Depth=4 × pool volume ÷ (PI × (diameter (length) ^ 2))
Depth 2=-depth 1 + 8 × pool volume ÷ (PI × diameter (length) × width)
Depth=4 × pool volume ÷ (PI × diameter (length) × width)
Water price=(1 ÷ 1000) × water cost (for this round pool) ÷ pool volume
Pool volume=(1 ÷ 1000) × water cost (for this oval pool) ÷ water price

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Pool type set to Above ground, Pool shape set to Round (circle), Diameter (length) = 30 m and Depth = 30 m. Working through the relationship above gives Depth 1 = -29.971706 m.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Depth 1 = -29.971706 m should be roughly the size you expected from Pool type set to Above ground and Pool shape set to Round (circle).

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Round pool volume calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Checking a supplier's figure against your own measurements
  • Ordering material and not wanting a second trip
  • Quoting a job where areas and quantities drive the price
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the diameter, the width and the pool volume — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Round pool volume calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns depth 1, derived from the diameter, the width and the pool volume. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Round pool volume calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the diameter, the width, the pool volume and the water cost (for this oval pool), which is 8 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter diameter (length) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Diameter (length) opens in meters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (2 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Depth 1 = -29.971706 m. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Round pool volume calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
